paragraphs.heading: A kind of atom
paragraphs.text: A chemical element is a type of atom, set apart by how many protons it holds. That proton count is called the atomic number. Oxygen's atomic number is 8, so every oxygen atom carries 8 protons in its nucleus. Atoms of one element can still differ in how many neutrons they have; these versions are called isotopes.

paragraphs.heading: Two meanings of one word
paragraphs.text: The word element is also used for a pure substance made only of that one kind of atom; oxygen gas, for instance, contains nothing but oxygen atoms. In the older sense, an element was a substance that chemical reactions cannot break down into component substances, and for most practical purposes that idea still holds. The two meanings can pull apart. Water (H₂O) contains the elements hydrogen and oxygen, yet it holds no dihydrogen (H₂) or dioxygen (O₂), because H₂O molecules differ from H₂ and O₂ molecules.

paragraphs.heading: How many there are
paragraphs.text: As of November 2016, a total of 118 elements were recognized by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC). The first 94 occur naturally on Earth, and the other 24 are synthetic, produced only in human-made nuclear reactions. Among the latest reported were element 118, now called oganesson, in October 2006, and element 117, tennessine, in April 2010. Finding and making further new elements is still an active field of research.

paragraphs.heading: Where elements come from
paragraphs.text: Hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements, were made in the Big Bang during the universe's first 20 minutes, in a mass ratio of about 3:1, along with tiny traces of lithium and beryllium. Nearly every other element found in nature was built by various natural kinds of nucleosynthesis. Elements are not fixed for good: nuclear reactions change an atom's atomic number and so turn it into another element. On Earth, ongoing radioactive decay keeps producing new atoms as daughter isotopes.

paragraphs.heading: The periodic table
paragraphs.text: Much of what we now know about elements grew out of work by the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, who published the first recognizable periodic table in 1869. The table lists elements by rising atomic number in rows called periods, while its columns, called groups, share physical and chemical properties that keep recurring. Because it sums up so many properties, chemists can use it to work out how elements relate and even to make predictions about extremely short-lived kinds of atoms not yet observed, along with compounds those unknown elements might form.

paragraphs.heading: Rarely found alone
paragraphs.text: Atoms can join to form molecules. Some elements make molecules only with their own kind: hydrogen atoms, for instance, pair up as H₂. Compounds are substances made from atoms of different elements. In nature, fewer than twenty elements, among them gold, platinum and the iron group metals, sometimes turn up uncombined as fairly pure minerals, while nearly all the rest exist on Earth as compounds or mixtures.
